slides.body: Clara Schumann's Three Romances, Op. 22 carry a dedication to the violinist Joseph Joachim.

slides.title: The trio, played with viola
slides.body: It was Joachim who read the viola part of Brahms's Trio in A minor, Op. 114 in rehearsal. That is the scoring heard here: viola, cello and piano.

ig.texto:
Two of the works Emilie-Anne plays on the 30th run back to the same man, and he isn't on the programme.

Joseph Joachim was twenty-two in 1853 when Clara Schumann dedicated her Three Romances to him. The two of them toured the pieces around Germany and Britain.

Nearly forty years later it was Joachim again, on viola this time, who read through the alternative scoring of Brahms's A minor Trio before Simrock printed it. That's the version we play: viola instead of clarinet.

Two pieces, nearly four decades apart, and the same violinist standing behind both of them.

30 October at The DiMenna Center.

Eight questions for Eric Moe

We have interviewed the composer Eric Moe because on 30 October we play his Laminar Flow in Upsidedown Creek at The DiMenna Center for Classical Music, in Currents, the first night of our twelfth season. The piece reached the programme through our open Call for Scores, and it sits that evening between Brahms and both Schumanns. Moe is a Guggenheim fellow, honoured by the American Academy of Arts and Letters, and co-directs Music on the Edge in Pittsburgh, which means he reads scores from the other side of the desk as well. Four weeks before the concert, we sent him eight questions.

Where did the title Laminar Flow in Upsidedown Creek come from?

“Laminar flow” is a term used to describe a fluid moving smoothly without eddies or turbulence. Upsidedown Creek is a short steep stream that dives off the Lake Plateau in the Beartooth Mountains of Montana into the Boulder River. (A hiking trail that ascends along the stream has a famous inverted sign at the trailhead). I admit that there’s not a lot of laminar flow in the actual Upsidedown Creek – I’ve been up and down the trail more than once – but my piece has a lot of quietly syncopated, gently flowing music with melodies that often turn upside down while re-examining themselves.

What was the initial idea or image behind the piece?

The visual idea of the piece came from looking at mountain streams and taking delight in the places where water sheets transparently over rocks and streambed. The kinetic idea of the piece came from performing and listening to suave tango-inspired compositions by Pablo Ortiz; a tango with three dancers.

What does “flow” mean to you musically?

“Flow” suggests more or less continual, more or less gentle rhythmic movement to me; a flow state is something I seek when writing music.

Is there something in the piece you would especially like listeners to notice or listen for?

It’s not essential to the enjoyment of the piece, but there’s a place near the end of the piece that I think is pretty cool. In the piece up to that point, there are essentially two melodic lines that the instruments take turns expressing. These two streams that have been flowing side by side – the soprano and bass lines – are finally joined by a third in a gentle apotheosis.

How does nature, science, or the physical world influence the way you think about music?

As the title suggests, I’m a nature-lover and a science-lover as well as a music-, art-, and literature-lover. I look to experience the sublime wherever I can find it in all its various forms and flavors.

What are some recent or upcoming projects you’re particularly excited about and would like to share?

My song cycle Girl Soup, a setting of surreal feminist poems by the poet Sawako Nakayasu, will be premiered on December 6 in New York by soprano Anna Elder and pianist Huizi Zhang (details forthcoming). A portrait CD, No Time Like The Present, including my new piano concerto has just been released by bmop/sound.

What are you most curious to hear in CreArtBox’s interpretation of the piece?

I’m very excited to hear what will be (as far as I know) only the second performance of the trio. The piece provides an intimate experience for the performers, who are (to an unusual degree) completing or echoing one another’s musical thoughts throughout. Additionally, I’m curious to hear Laminar Flow in the context of pieces I have loved and studied for many years (Schumann, Brahms).

You co-direct Music on the Edge and have been programming new music in Pittsburgh for years. From the other side of the desk: what makes you say yes to a score you have never heard of?

In considering new work for programming, in addition to pieces with engaging, unsurprising qualities – rhythmic interest (unrelated to tempo, btw), fresh musical ideas, dramatic pacing – I admire and favor pieces that will provide a rewarding experience for the performer. This doesn’t mean that the piece has to be easy or even idiomatically written for the instruments – after all, overcoming challenges is part of the joy of musicmaking. But if the performers are excited about the piece, then listeners are bound to be excited as well.

posts.title: Five days in Kuopio
posts.excerpt: Kuopio Conservatory asked for a look at how we work rather than a recital, so we gave them a concert, a week of masterclasses, and a workshop that ended with a cellist playing alone in a darkened hall, surrounded by lamps and projections responding to her music.

slides.title: Five days in Kuopio

ig.texto:
Five days in Kuopio, Finland 🇫🇮

We were invited by Kuopio Conservatory to share something a little different. Not just a concert or masterclasses, but a look at how we work at CreArtBox, bringing music together with light, video, and other visual elements.

Guillermo and Josefina performed at the Kuopio Music Centre, with music by Lili Boulanger, Messiaen, Janáček, Debussy, Clara Schumann, Falla, and Frank Martin. We also spent the week teaching flute and piano masterclasses and talking with students about everything that goes into making a performance.

One of our favorite moments was the workshop. We experimented with how light, movement, and video can change the way we experience music. We looped a few bars of Falla, moved around the space, played with different lighting ideas, and ended up with a cellist playing alone in a darkened hall, surrounded by lamps and projections responding to her music.

It was great to see how quickly the students started coming up with their own ideas.

A big thank you to everyone at Kuopio Conservatory for inviting us and being so open to experimenting with us. We'd love to come back!

We wrote a little more about the experience (and shared some photos) on our website. Full story at the link in bio!

posts.excerpt: He sketched the Piano Quartet between 24 and 30 October 1842 and copied it out in November. We play it on 30 October, a hundred and eighty-four years to the day after he put the last sketch down.

slides.title: Sketched 30 October 1842. Played 30 October 2026.

ig.texto:
We only noticed this while putting the programme notes together.

1842 was Schumann's chamber music year: three string quartets, the Piano Quintet, this Piano Quartet, and the trio that later became the Phantasiestücke.

He sketched the Quartet between 24 and 30 October, then spent most of November copying it out.

We play it on 30 October. A hundred and eighty-four years to the day after he put the last sketch down.

Nobody planned that. We just liked the piece.

posts.title: He had announced he was finished. Then he heard one clarinettist.
posts.excerpt: In December 1890 he told his publisher he was done composing. Then in March 1891 he heard a clarinettist in Meiningen, and that summer he wrote two more pieces. We play the first movement of one of them on 30 October.

slides.title: He had announced he was finished. Then he heard one clarinettist.

ig.texto:
A small Brahms story.

By the end of 1890 he had written to his publisher saying he was finished composing. He meant it. He had put his affairs in order.

Then in March 1891 he heard Richard Mühlfeld, the principal clarinettist at the Meiningen court orchestra, and changed his mind. That summer at Bad Ischl he wrote two new pieces for him: the Clarinet Quintet and the A minor Trio.

Here's the part we like. When Simrock published the Trio in 1892, Brahms offered a viola part as an alternative to the clarinet, and both versions were tried out in rehearsal before it went to print, with Joachim on viola.

That's the version Matthew, Julia and Josefina play on the 30th.

posts.title: She wrote these in 1853. After 1854 she wrote almost nothing new.
posts.excerpt: She wrote the Three Romances in 1853 and dedicated them to Joachim. Brahms knocked on the door that September; Robert collapsed the following February. After that she wrote almost nothing new.

slides.title: She wrote these in 1853. After 1854 she wrote almost nothing new.

ig.texto:
We've been working on Clara Schumann's Three Romances.

She wrote them in Düsseldorf in 1853 and dedicated them to Joseph Joachim, who was twenty-two at the time. The two of them toured the pieces around Germany and Britain, including a performance for King George V, who by Joachim's account loved them.

The dates are the part that stays with you. Brahms, twenty years old, arrived at the Schumanns' door on 30 September that same year. Robert collapsed the following February. From then on Clara wrote almost nothing new and gave her working life to performing and to editing his music.

These Romances are among the last original pieces she wrote. Eleven minutes, played by Emilie-Anne and Josefina.

30 October at DiMenna.

posts.title: Schumann asks the cellist to retune mid-movement
posts.excerpt: The slow movement of the Piano Quartet ends on a low B flat the cello cannot reach, so Schumann has the player tune the bottom string down a whole step mid-movement, hold the note under the final bars, and tune it back up for the finale.

slides.title: Schumann asks the cellist to retune mid-movement

ig.texto:
The piece we're most looking forward to, and a detail worth watching for.

Robert Schumann's Piano Quartet in E flat, Op. 47. Clara gave the public premiere at the Leipzig Gewandhaus on 8 December 1844, with Ferdinand David on violin and Niels Gade on viola. Almost two centuries later it closes our night.

The slow movement is the one. Schumann hands the melody to the cello, and then ends the movement underneath everything on a low B flat, a note the cello does not have.

So he writes in the fix. The cellist tunes the bottom C string down a whole step in the middle of the movement, holds that note under the final bars, and tunes it back up in time for the finale.

It serves the music and it inconveniences the cellist, and Schumann asked for it anyway.

ig.texto:
Not everything we do needs a ticket.

Alongside the New York Series we work with public libraries, schools and community institutions, in New York and beyond. A library concert is a completely different thing from a hall: people walk in, sit down, and listen for half an hour without planning an evening around it.

And for the concerts that are ticketed, cost shouldn't be what stops you. We run subsidised seats through the NYC Culture Pass and with the Queens Public Library. Ticket revenue has never covered what a concert costs to put on, and donor support is what makes that possible.

If the price is the reason you're not coming, write to us at info@creartbox.nyc. Someone answers.

posts.excerpt: Tenemos un archivo navegable por años, lugares y formatos, con foto y vídeo profesional de cada acción. No es vanidad ni burocracia: para un proyecto rural, el archivo es la herramienta de supervivencia.

slides.title: Por qué un festival pequeño documenta todo lo que hace
1. Porque es la prueba de que existimos
slides.body: Empecemos por la más práctica y la menos romántica. Somos una asociación sin ánimo de lucro con sede en una aldea de cien habitantes. Cada año tenemos que convencer a instituciones, patrocinadores y ayuntamientos de que merece la pena apoyar esto.

slides.title: 2. Porque los sitios donde tocamos son frágiles
slides.body: Esta es la razón que más nos pesa. Tocamos en monasterios con problemas de conservación. En paneras de madera que llevan siglos aguantando y que dependen de que alguien las cuide. En hórreos que se caen en silencio, uno a uno, cuando nadie los usa.

Grabar un concierto no es hacer cine
slides.body: Casi todos los festivales graban sus conciertos. Se pone una cámara al fondo, quizá dos, y se sube el resultado a YouTube. Es útil: sirve de prueba, de memoria y de material para pedir subvenciones.

slides.title: Taramundi: el pueblo de los cuchillos artesanos donde sonó Mussorgsky
Dos oficios que se parecen más de lo que parece
slides.body: Un cuchillo de Taramundi y una sonata de Telemann tienen mucho en común, aunque suene raro decirlo. Los dos se aprenden con las manos. No hay manera de aprender a forjar leyendo sobre forja, igual que no hay manera de aprender a tocar leyendo sobre música.

slides.title: El programa: tres siglos y tres países
slides.body: Merece la pena mirar la elección, porque no es casual. Telemann, alemán del barroco, prolífico y luminoso: el artesano perfecto de la música, alguien que produjo con una regularidad de taller.

Qué demonios significa eso
slides.body: Vamos despacio, porque la idea merece el esfuerzo. Un menhir es una piedra grande que alguien puso de pie hace miles de años. No sirve para nada práctico: no es un muro, ni un refugio, ni una herramienta.

slides.title: Por qué esto nos toca de lleno
slides.body: Cuando encontramos esta idea, tuvimos la sensación incómoda y agradable de que alguien había teorizado lo que nosotros hacíamos por instinto.

posts.title: Una ballena encima de una montaña: la noche más onírica de ADAR
posts.excerpt: Un pueblo despierta y encuentra una ballena tendida en la cima de la montaña. Con esa leyenda, el ensemble Ballarte llenó de música antigua y realismo mágico el monasterio de San Antolín de Bedón.

slides.title: Una ballena encima de una montaña: la noche más onírica de ADAR
De dónde sale la ballena
slides.body: La leyenda no es asturiana. Está inspirada en el perfil de la montaña de Montserrat, en Cataluña: ese macizo de formas redondeadas que, mirado con la cabeza adecuada, puede parecer un animal enorme dormido.

slides.title: Trovadores del siglo XXI
slides.body: The Whale es un espectáculo de varias capas: música, interpretación, instalación escénica y elementos audiovisuales. Pero su ambición declarada es más antigua que todo eso.

Una casa restaurada en la montaña
slides.body: La sede de ADAR es una casa restaurada en la montaña del occidente asturiano. Y la mejor manera de describirla es por lo que no es: No es una sala de conciertos. No tiene taquilla, ni butacas numeradas, ni camerinos.

slides.title: Por qué eso cambia el trabajo
slides.body: Quienes residen en Leiguarda 47 conviven, comen juntos y desarrollan sus proyectos codo con codo. Puede sonar a detalle logístico. Es, en realidad, el corazón del método. Piensa cómo funciona normalmente.

posts.excerpt: Acaba la sexta edición. Un buen momento para mirar atrás sin nostalgia y contar, con honestidad, qué hemos aprendido en estos años y hacia dónde va el proyecto.

slides.title: Seis ediciones de ADAR: lo que hemos aprendido llevando la música donde no se la espera
1. El nivel no hay que bajarlo. Nunca.
slides.body: Al empezar, más de una vez nos preguntaron si "para el pueblo" no convendría una programación más ligera, más fácil. Seis ediciones después lo tenemos clarísimo: no. El público del medio rural no quiere una versión descafeinada de la cultura.

slides.title: 2. El sitio importa tanto como el programa.
slides.body: Aprendimos que un concierto en una iglesia de aldea, en un parador, en un alto de monte, no es el mismo concierto que en un auditorio. El lugar entra en la música.

posts.excerpt: En ADAR el concierto no acaba cuando se apagan las luces. Acaba con una espicha, sidra en mano, artistas y público mezclados. Y eso no es el postre: es parte de la idea.

slides.title: La espicha después del último acorde: por qué la música y la sidra terminan juntas
Qué es una espicha (por si no eres de aquí)
slides.body: Para quien no sea asturiano: una espicha es una reunión en torno a la sidra. El nombre viene del espiche, el palo que tapa el agujero del tonel; "espichar" es abrirlo y empezar a escanciar.

slides.title: Por qué la ponemos al final de un concierto
slides.body: Podría parecer un simple detalle simpático, el "vino de honor" de toda la vida. Es mucho más que eso. La espicha hace un trabajo que ninguna otra parte del festival puede hacer: aplana la jerarquía.

slides.title: Cómo escuchar «sweet air» de David Lang (y perderle el miedo a la música contemporánea)
Quién es David Lang
slides.body: David Lang es un compositor estadounidense, premio Pulitzer de música en 2008 por su The Little Match Girl Passion, y una de las cabezas del colectivo Bang on a Can, que lleva décadas acercando la música de hoy a públicos que creían que no era para ellos.

slides.title: El error: escucharla como si fuera Beethoven
slides.body: El malentendido casi siempre viene de aquí. Escuchamos música contemporánea esperando lo que nos dio la música del XIX: un tema que reconoces, un clímax, una resolución con moraleja. Y cuando eso no llega, concluimos que "no la entendemos".

posts.excerpt: Žilvinas Brazauskas tocó en Leiguarda un instrumento que empezó siendo un juguete de pastores lituanos hace cuatro siglos. La historia de la birbynė es también la historia de por qué el mundo cabe en una aldea.

slides.title: Una birbynė en Leiguarda: cuando una flauta de pastor lituano suena en una iglesia asturiana
Un juguete de pastores del año 1625
slides.body: La birbynė no nació en un conservatorio. Nació en el campo. Es un instrumento de viento lituano, primo lejano del clarinete, hecho en origen con paja, corteza o cuerno de animal, con una lengüeta simple o doble.

slides.title: De una aldea lituana a otra asturiana
slides.body: Piénsalo un momento. Un instrumento que empezó siendo el entretenimiento de un chaval cuidando ovejas en Lituania acabó, cuatro siglos después, sonando bajo las bóvedas de una iglesia de Belmonte de Miranda, delante de vecinos de Leiguarda.

posts.excerpt: El 12 de agosto de 2026 Asturias vivió el primer eclipse total de sol sobre la España peninsular en 121 años. Lo esperamos tocando, en un alto de Belmonte, con la música pensada para el instante exacto de la sombra.

slides.title: El día que Asturias se quedó a oscuras: crónica del concierto del eclipse
Tocar contra el reloj del cielo
slides.body: Un eclipse no admite ensayo con público, ni segundo pase. La totalidad estaba prevista para las 20:27, con el sol a apenas diez grados sobre el horizonte, casi rozando el mar por el oeste.

slides.title: Música para la sombra
slides.body: La pregunta que nos hicimos al diseñar el programa fue sencilla y difícil: ¿qué se toca mientras el mundo se queda a oscuras? No quisimos ilustrar el eclipse ni "acompañarlo" como quien pone banda sonora.
